knowledge_fragments.content: The diagnostic criteria of stroke were formulated according to the “2016 China Stroke Diagnosis and Treatment Consensus.” Diagnostic points are as follows: ① acute onset; ② focal neurological deficit (such as weakness or numbness of one side of face or limb, language disorder); a few patients have comprehensive neurological deficit, which may be accompanied by headache, vomiting, elevated blood pressure, and different degrees of consciousness disorder; ③ symptoms or signs of unlimited duration (when imaging shows responsible lesions) or lasting more than 24 h (when imaging shows no responsible lesions); ④ stroke diagnosed by CT or MRI of the head, with non-cerebral vascular causes excluded.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 23-year-old Caucasian female was admitted to the Department of Neurology at the end of September due to tremors in her hands and paresthesia extending to her forearms, without any upper limb weakness. She also experienced severe pain in the mid-cervical region. From May to September, she had episodes of nausea and vertigo, along with transient episodes of double vision when focusing on distant objects. Most symptoms decreased in intensity by September, except for the limb tremor, cervical pain, and double vision. A medical interview revealed a 2-day fever episode in May, during which she might have been exposed to a tick bite in a forested area, although she did not recall the bite. Her family history was negative for neurological or chronic familial diseases. She was not on any permanent medication, did not smoke, and did not consume alcohol or drugs. There was no history of trauma, infections, or intoxication, and she was otherwise in good health. A review of her systems was negative. knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 27-year-old male, employed as an electrical mechanic with extensive travel history to Germany, China, Russia, and South Korea, initially sought medical attention for worsening back pain. He was admitted to an orthopedic department due to back pain and a developing neurological deficit in the lower extremities. MRI of the spine identified an atypical mass in the left upper lung lobe encasing the Th3-Th4 vertebrae. CT of the thorax revealed a 3.9 cm x 2.9 cm mass in the left upper lung lobe. Histological analysis of a biopsy from the mass showed the presence of histiocytes, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Following neurosurgical intervention, the neurological deficit improved, and the patient was discharged. The lung mass was surgically removed in a subsequent operation, and histological examination confirmed similar findings. Infectious agents including mycobacteria, legionella, Borrelia burgdorferi, pneumocystis, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), herpes simplex virus, human immunodeficiency virus-1/2, parvovirus, respiratory viruses, cytomegalovirus (CMV), other bacteria, stool pathogens, and urinary histoplasma antigen were excluded. knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 36-year-old male presented with shortness of breath and swelling in the lower extremities for the past 2 weeks. The patient also reported experiencing intermittent fever over the last 2 months. Upon admission, vital signs included a heart rate of 103 beats per minute, blood pressure of 122/47 mmHg, and a temperature of 37.2°C. Cardiac examination identified a pandiastolic murmur in the aortic region. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated NT-proBNP level of 4492.0 pg/mL.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 25-year-old woman reported a sudden loss of vision in her right eye 5 years ago, followed by intermittent body jerking for the past 10 months. She experienced a gradual onset of weakness in her left upper limb 10 months ago and in her left lower limb 8 months ago. Two months ago, she had a sudden decrease in vision in her left eye, and for the past 2 weeks, she has had urinary incontinence. Upon examination, she was conscious but disoriented to place and time, recognizing only her husband. Her speech was disrupted by myoclonic jerks affecting her entire body, more pronounced on the left side, occurring every 8–10 seconds with slow relaxation. Muscle strength was rated at 4/5 on the left side, deep tendon reflexes were 3+ bilaterally, and plantar reflexes were downgoing.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 71-year-old male from Madrid, Spain, presented with a 2-month history of dysphonia. He has a 30-year history of smoking and underwent a liver transplant 8 years ago due to liver cirrhosis, currently on chronic immunosuppressant therapy with mycophenolate mofetil. The patient exhibited symptoms including dysphonia, dysphagia, odynophagia, autophony, fatigue, anorexia, and a weight loss of over 20 kg in the past 6 months. Fiber-optic laryngoscopy identified a vegetative lesion on the lingual surface of the epiglottis, extending to the epiglottic vallecula. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan showed increased soft tissue size on the lingual surface of the epiglottis.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Histoplasmosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Histoplasmosis.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Subacute Histoplasmosis

knowledge_fragments.content: Electrodiagnostic criteria: Motor conduction criteria fulfillment is necessary for at least two upper limb nerves to confirm the clinical diagnosis of distal CIDP. The distal negative peak compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude should be at least 1 mV. When criteria are fulfilled in two lower limb nerves but not upper limb nerves or if criteria are fulfilled in only one upper limb nerve, the maximum diagnostic certainty is possible distal CIDP. Additionally, sensory conduction abnormalities must be present in at least two nerves.

He was admitted to an orthopedic department due to back pain and a developing neurological deficit in the lower extremities. MRI of the spine identified an atypical mass in the left upper lung lobe encasing the Th3-Th4 vertebrae. CT of the thorax revealed a 3.9 cm x 2.9 cm mass in the left upper lung lobe. Histological analysis of a biopsy from the mass showed the presence of histiocytes, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Following neurosurgical intervention, the neurological deficit improved, and the patient was discharged. The lung mass was surgically removed in a subsequent operation, and histological examination confirmed similar findings. knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 36-year-old male presented with shortness of breath and swelling in the lower extremities for the past 2 weeks. The patient also reported experiencing intermittent fever over the last 2 months. Upon admission, vital signs included a heart rate of 103 beats per minute, blood pressure of 122/47 mmHg, and a temperature of 37.2°C. Cardiac examination identified a pandiastolic murmur in the aortic region. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated NT-proBNP level of 4492.0 pg/mL.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis

knowledge_fragments.content: Electrodiagnostic criteria: Motor conduction criteria fulfillment is necessary for at least two upper limb nerves to confirm the clinical diagnosis of distal CIDP. The distal negative peak compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude should be at least 1 mV. When criteria are fulfilled in two lower limb nerves but not upper limb nerves or if criteria are fulfilled in only one upper limb nerve, the maximum diagnostic certainty is possible distal CIDP. Additionally, sensory conduction abnormalities must be present in at least two nerves.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 25-year-old woman reported a sudden loss of vision in her right eye 5 years ago, followed by intermittent body jerking for the past 10 months. She experienced a gradual onset of weakness in her left upper limb 10 months ago and in her left lower limb 8 months ago. Two months ago, she had a sudden decrease in vision in her left eye, and for the past 2 weeks, she has had urinary incontinence. Upon examination, she was conscious but disoriented to place and time, recognizing only her husband. Her speech was disrupted by myoclonic jerks affecting her entire body, more pronounced on the left side, occurring every 8–10 seconds with slow relaxation. Muscle strength was rated at 4/5 on the left side, deep tendon reflexes were 3+ bilaterally, and plantar reflexes were downgoing.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 71-year-old male from Madrid, Spain, presented with a 2-month history of dysphonia. He has a 30-year history of smoking and underwent a liver transplant 8 years ago due to liver cirrhosis, currently on chronic immunosuppressant therapy with mycophenolate mofetil. The patient exhibited symptoms including dysphonia, dysphagia, odynophagia, autophony, fatigue, anorexia, and a weight loss of over 20 kg in the past 6 months. Fiber-optic laryngoscopy identified a vegetative lesion on the lingual surface of the epiglottis, extending to the epiglottic vallecula. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan showed increased soft tissue size on the lingual surface of the epiglottis.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Histoplasmosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Histoplasmosis.

tree.case_summary:
A 55-year-old male bodybuilder presents to the emergency department with weakness of his right arm. The patient states he has experienced these symptoms for a few weeks; however, today his hand felt so weak he dropped his cup of tea. The patient has a medical history of diabetes. He drinks 2-7 alcoholic drinks per day and has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes per day since he was 25. The patient uses anabolic steroids. He has lost 17 pounds since he last came to the emergency department 1 month ago. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 177/108 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals decreased sensation in the right arm and 2/5 strength in the right arm and 5/5 strength in in the left arm. The patient states that he is experiencing a dull aching and burning pain in his right arm during the exam. Symptoms are not changed with changes in head and neck position. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Apical lung tumor
B. Brachial plexopathy
C. Cerebral infarction
D. Scalenus anticus syndrome
E. Subclavian steal syndrome
